column5: Defamation Act 2013 s1: a statement is not defamatory unless publishing it has caused or is likely to cause serious harm to the claimant's reputation; for a business that trades for profit, serious harm means serious financial loss. s15: a 'statement' includes words, pictures, visual images and gestures, so slides and props count as well as the spoken word.

Defamation Act 2013 defences: s2 truth (the imputation is substantially true; a few unproved minor points do not sink it if they do not seriously harm the claimant); s3 honest opinion (the statement was opinion, it indicated the basis of the opinion, and an honest person could have held it on facts existing at the time; defeated if the speaker did not actually hold it); s4 public interest (a statement on a matter of public interest that the speaker reasonably believed it was in the public interest to publish). For a persuasive speech about a named person or business: state the facts you rely on, keep opinions labelled as opinions, and only say what you believe and can support.

Defamation Act 2013 links to the ethics module: the textbook's ethics pyramid asks speakers not to make claims they cannot support; in English and Welsh law, truth and honest opinion based on stated facts are also the main defences if a claim about a named person seriously harms their reputation.

Defamation Act 2013 s17: the Act extends to England and Wales only, apart from a few sections (6, 7(9), 15) that also extend to Scotland; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own defamation law, which this course has not read. The text read is the Act as enacted, and later amendments were not checked.

Defamation Act 2013 ss5-13 cover website operators, peer-reviewed journals, privileged reports, the single publication rule, jurisdiction, jury trial and court orders; these matter to publishers rather than to a speaker preparing a talk.
